<Rep. Robert Garcia>: Since the beginning of his second term, President Trump and his allies in Congress have sustained an unrelenting attack on the Inspector General community. The assault began with the illegal mass firing of Inspectors General during President Trump's first month in office in 2025. Since that time, President Trump has left many Inspector General positions vacant and installed overtly partisan appointees in others. The government-wide overhaul in Offices of Inspectors General has generated a culture of fear. Independent oversight has been blocked in order to deliberately facilitate illegal activity and corruption by or within federal agencies.
This Administration's assault on the Inspector General community continues with the Office of Management and Budget's practice to apportion Congressionally appropriated funds to the Council on Inspectors General for Integrity and Efficiency (CIGIE) quarterly rather than annually. CIGIE, an entity created in statute, provides crucial services to the Inspector General community, including training and back-end services for websites and IT. CIGIE, however, has drawn the ire of Trump and his allies in Congress over its peer investigative function, the Integrity Committee. The apportionment process is controlled by the Office of Management and Budget, which must apportion funds to agencies before they can use it. CIGIE is an indispensable enabler for the work of Inspectors General across agencies. It facilitates information sharing and encourages Offices of Inspector General to communicate and share best practices. The inter-office function of CIGIE is also what made it a natural home for the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee (PRAC).
The PRAC has garnered wide bipartisan support for its work examining pandemic-era programs. The PRAC's analytics ability, bolstered by robust data-sharing agreements between agencies, gives it a unique edge in both identifying fraud schemes and clawing back money claimed by fraudsters. The PRAC stands as an exemplar of what smart oversight can accomplish with strong bipartisan support. Last year, the PRAC's authorization was extended to September 30, 2034, and its remit was expanded with the support of Oversight Democrats.
H.R. 8312 would move the PRAC from CIGIE to the Department of Treasury. This would effectively clear the way for the Trump Administration to further undermine or even completely defund CIGIE by removing a key bipartisan initiative from its purview.
At the Department of the Treasury, PRAC would become the third Office of Inspector General in that department. H.R. 8312 would create unnecessary issues with jurisdiction for this new Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery, without any offsetting benefits.
Committee Democrats support creating a permanent home for the PRAC and giving it more power to coordinate and assist Offices of Inspector General in performing their functions, but we cannot support a bill that would give the Trump Administration the ability to pull the rug out from under the rest of the Inspector General community. Should the Administration decide to completely withhold apportionment for CIGIE, as it did in October 2025, it would be a disaster for Offices of Inspector General and Congress alike: many oversight websites would cease to function, preventing us from accessing thousands of reports on how to improve government programs; law enforcement officers in small Offices of Inspector General would have no way to get their required law enforcement training; and auditors and investigators across the oversight community would be left without a way to get the training necessary to perform their duties. H.R. 8312 purports to further the effort to prevent fraud--a worthy and essential effort--but it does so at too great a cost.
Committee Democrats strongly oppose this legislation, which uses the facade of fraud prevention to undermine an entire ecosystem intended to hold the executive branch accountable.
Robert Garcia,
Ranking Member.
